pairs.source_text: Iuri operam daturum prius nosse oportet, unde nomen iuris descendat. est autem a iustitia appellatum: nam, ut eleganter celsus definit, ius est ars boni et aequi.
pairs.question: Quibus verbis Celsus, ut Ulpianus refert, ius definit?
pairs.answer: Ius est ars boni et aequi.
pairs.question_en: In what words does Celsus, as Ulpian reports, define law (ius)?
pairs.answer_en: Law is the art of the good and the equitable.
pairs.derivation: The single most-quoted definition of ius in Roman law, attributed by Ulpian to Celsus. Closed-book famous maxim, entity-anchored to Celsus, short verifiable answer present verbatim ('ius est ars boni et aequi').

pairs.source_text: Ius naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit: nam ius istud non humani generis proprium, sed omnium animalium, quae in terra, quae in mari nascuntur, avium quoque commune est.
pairs.question: Quomodo Ulpianus ius naturale definit?
pairs.question_en: How does Ulpian define natural law (ius naturale)?
pairs.answer_en: That which nature has taught all animals.
pairs.derivation: Ulpian's famous definition of ius naturale as the law nature taught all animals, not only mankind. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + ius naturale, short answer verbatim from the source.

pairs.source_text: et cum uno naturali nomine homines appellaremur, iure gentium tria genera esse coeperunt: liberi et his contrarium servi et tertium genus liberti, id est hi qui desierant esse servi.
pairs.question: Quae tria genera hominum iure gentium orta esse Ulpianus scribit?
pairs.question_en: Which three classes of men does Ulpian say arose by the law of nations (ius gentium)?
pairs.derivation: Ulpian: under ius gentium three classes of men arose — liberi, servi, liberti. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + ius gentium, three named-entity answer verbatim. Indirect statement (orta esse) governed by scribit.

pairs.source_text: Ius praetorium est, quod praetores introduxerunt adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia propter utilitatem publicam. quod et honorarium dicitur ad honorem praetorum sic nominatum.
pairs.question: Cuius rei gratia praetores ius praetorium introduxisse Papinianus scribit?
pairs.answer: Adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia.
pairs.question_en: For what purpose does Papinian say the praetors introduced praetorian law?
pairs.answer_en: For the sake of aiding, supplementing, or correcting the civil law.
pairs.derivation: Papinian's classic triad of the purposes of ius praetorium (adiuvandi, supplendi, corrigendi iuris civilis). Closed-book, anchored to Papinian + ius praetorium, answer verbatim. Indirect statement (introduxisse) governed by scribit.

pairs.source_text: Iustitia est constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
pairs.question: Quomodo Ulpianus iustitiam definit?
pairs.answer: Constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
pairs.answer_en: The constant and perpetual will to render to each his own right.
pairs.derivation: The canonical definition of iustitia (later opening Justinian's Institutes), quoted here from Ulpian. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + iustitia, short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Iuris praecepta sunt haec: honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
pairs.question: Quae sunt tria iuris praecepta secundum Ulpianum?
pairs.answer: Honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
pairs.question_en: What are the three precepts of law according to Ulpian?
pairs.answer_en: To live honourably, to harm no one, to render to each his own.
pairs.derivation: Ulpian's three iuris praecepta, among the most famous formulas in Western law. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + iuris praecepta, three-part answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Postea aucta ad aliquem modum civitate ipsum romulum traditur populum in triginta partes divisisse, quas partes curias appellavit propterea quod tunc reipublicae curam per sententias partium earum expediebat.
pairs.question: In quot partes Romulus populum divisisse traditur, quas curias appellavit, ut Pomponius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Into how many parts is Romulus said to have divided the people, which he called curiae, as Pomponius writes?
pairs.derivation: From Pomponius's history of law: Romulus divided the people into 30 curiae. Closed-book, anchored to Romulus + curiae, single number answer (triginta) verbatim; traditur keeps the 'it is reported' frame (nom.+inf. construction).

pairs.source_text: Placuit publica auctoritate decem constitui viros, per quos peterentur leges a graecis civitatibus et civitas fundaretur legibus: quas in tabulas eboreas perscriptas pro rostris composuerunt, ut possint leges apertius percipi. qui ipsi animadverterunt aliquid deesse istis primis legibus ideoque sequenti anno alias duas ad easdem tabulas adiecerunt: et ita ex accedenti appellatae sunt leges duodecim tabularum.
pairs.question: Quot viri publica auctoritate constituti sunt, ut leges duodecim tabularum conderentur, secundum Pomponium?
pairs.question_en: How many men were appointed by public authority to establish the law of the Twelve Tables, according to Pomponius?
pairs.derivation: Pomponius: ten men (decemviri) were appointed and composed the Twelve Tables (two more tables added the following year giving the name). Closed-book, anchored to the Twelve Tables + decemviri, number answer (decem) verbatim from 'decem constitui viros'.

pairs.source_text: itaque dictatores proditi sunt, a quibus nec provocandi ius fuit et quibus etiam capitis animadversio data est. hunc magistratum, quoniam summam potestatem habebat, non erat fas ultra sextum mensem retineri.
pairs.question: Ultra quot menses dictaturam retineri fas non erat secundum Pomponium?
pairs.question_en: Beyond how many months was it not lawful to retain the dictatorship, according to Pomponius?
pairs.derivation: Pomponius: the dictatorship, holding supreme power, could not lawfully be held beyond six months. Closed-book institutional fact, anchored to the dictatorship, number answer verbatim ('ultra sextum mensem').

pairs.source_text: Post hos fuerunt publius mucius et brutus et manilius, qui fundaverunt ius civile. ex his publius mucius etiam decem libellos reliquit, brutus septem, manilius tres.
pairs.question: Qui tres iuris periti ius civile fundavisse a Pomponio dicuntur?
pairs.question_en: Which three jurists are said by Pomponius to have founded the civil law?
pairs.derivation: Pomponius names the three 'founders of ius civile' (qui fundaverunt ius civile): Publius Mucius Scaevola, Brutus, Manilius. Closed-book in legal history, three named-entity answer verbatim; dicuntur + nom.+inf. (fundavisse).

pairs.source_text: Post hos fuit tiberius coruncanius, ut dixi, qui primus profiteri coepit: cuius tamen scriptum nullum exstat, sed responsa complura et memorabilia eius fuerunt.
pairs.question: Quis primus ius publice profiteri coepisse a Pomponio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pomponius, was the first to begin teaching law publicly?
pairs.derivation: Pomponius: Tiberius Coruncanius was the first to teach/give responsa publicly (profiteri). Closed-book historical fact, single named-entity answer, supported by 'qui primus profiteri coepit' (cf. 1.2.2.35 'ante Tiberium Coruncanium publice professum neminem').

pairs.source_text: Legis virtus haec est imperare vetare permittere punire.
pairs.question: Quae sunt quattuor legis virtutes secundum Modestinum?
pairs.question_en: What are the four powers (functions) of law according to Modestinus?
pairs.answer_en: To command, to forbid, to permit, to punish.
pairs.derivation: Modestinus's four functions of law (imperare, vetare, permittere, punire). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Modestinus + lex, four-part answer verbatim.

pairs.locus: Justinian, Digesta 1.3.31 (Ulpianus 13 ad l. iul. et pap.)
pairs.source_text: Princeps legibus solutus est: augusta autem licet legibus soluta non est, principes tamen eadem illi privilegia tribuunt, quae ipsi habent.
pairs.question: Quid de principe quoad leges Ulpianus affirmat?
pairs.question_en: What does Ulpian assert about the emperor with respect to the laws?
pairs.answer_en: That the emperor is freed from (not bound by) the laws.
pairs.derivation: The maxim 'princeps legibus solutus est', foundational to later theories of sovereignty, stated here by Ulpian. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer; indirect statement (Principem... solutum esse) governed by affirmat, supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem: utpote cum lege regia, quae de imperio eius lata est, populus ei et in eum omne suum imperium et potestatem conferat.
pairs.question: Quam vim habere id quod principi placuit Ulpianus tradit?
pairs.question_en: What force does Ulpian record that whatever pleases the emperor has?
pairs.derivation: Ulpian's maxim 'quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem'. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer 'legis vigorem' verbatim; indirect statement (id... habere) governed by tradit.

pairs.source_text: Omne ius quo utimur vel ad personas pertinet vel ad res vel ad actiones.
pairs.question: Ad quae tria omne ius quo utimur pertinere Gaius scribit?
pairs.answer: Ad personas, ad res, ad actiones.
pairs.question_en: To which three things does Gaius say that all the law we use pertains?
pairs.answer_en: To persons, to things, and to actions.
pairs.derivation: Gaius's tripartite division of all law into personae, res, actiones — the organizing scheme of his Institutes. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, three-part answer verbatim; indirect statement (pertinere) governed by scribit.

pairs.source_text: In orbe romano qui sunt ex constitutione imperatoris antonini cives romani effecti sunt.
pairs.question: Cuius imperatoris constitutione omnes qui in orbe Romano erant cives Romani facti sunt, ut Ulpianus scribit?
pairs.question_en: By the constitution of which emperor did all who were in the Roman world become Roman citizens, as Ulpian writes?
pairs.derivation: Ulpian's record of the Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212), by which Caracalla (Antoninus) granted citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire. Closed-book famous historical fact, anchored to the emperor Antoninus, single named-entity answer verbatim ('ex constitutione imperatoris Antonini').
